issue.issue_text: Whether the evidentiary value of a dying declaration is destroyed when the original document is stolen from the court file, especially when the Judicial Magistrate who recorded it testifies to its contents.

facts: The original document of the dying declaration was stolen from the court's judicial record.
The Judicial Magistrate who had recorded the dying declaration testified in court about its contents.
The court noted that it was unnecessary to determine who was responsible for the theft of the document in order to decide the issue.
law: The text does not cite a specific law but establishes the principle that the contents of a lost or stolen document can be proven through secondary evidence.
A dying declaration is a significant piece of evidence, and its value is not inherently tied only to the physical presence of the original document.
application: The court directly relied on the testimony of the Judicial Magistrate as valid evidence of the dying declaration's contents.

The court reasoned that because the magistrate who recorded the statement was able to testify, "the mere fact that the original dying declaration had been stolen from the file, could not destroy its value."
The magistrate's evidence effectively substituted for the missing original document, allowing the court to consider the substance of the declaration.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that the evidentiary value of the dying declaration was not destroyed because the Judicial Magistrate who recorded it testified to its contents, thereby proving what was in the stolen original document.

issue.issue_text: Whether the evidentiary value of a dying declaration is diminished because the investigating officer was allowed to make a copy of it.

facts: A Judicial Magistrate recorded a dying declaration.
The defense argued that the Magistrate's credibility was questionable because he allowed the investigating police officer to make a copy of the dying declaration.
The defense contended that this action showed the Magistrate was subservient to the police, which should diminish the value of the declaration.
law: A dying declaration is not a confidential document that must be kept secret from the investigating officer.
application: The Court found no reason why allowing the investigating officer to copy the dying declaration would reflect negatively on the Magistrate or the declaration's value.
The Court reasoned that the dying declaration could "legitimately serve as a guide in further investigation."
Therefore, it was proper for the investigating officer to have a copy to assist with the investigation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the evidentiary value of a dying declaration is not diminished simply because the investigating officer was permitted to make a copy of it, as it is not a confidential document and can be used to guide the investigation.

cases.case_name: Kushal Rao v. State of Bombay
cases.principle: It cannot be laid down as an absolute rule of law that a dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of conviction unless it is corroborated; each case must be determined on its own facts, keeping in view the circumstances in which the dying declaration was made.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: It is not an absolute rule of law that a dying declaration cannot form the sole basis of a conviction unless it is corroborated. A dying declaration is not a weaker kind of evidence; it stands on the same footing as other evidence and must be judged on the facts and surrounding circumstances of each case. The court has an obligation to closely scrutinize all attendant circumstances when testing its reliability.
obiter: A dying declaration is admitted in evidence as an exception to the general rule against the admissibility of hearsay evidence on the principle of necessity.
A dying declaration is not a deposition in court, is not made on oath, is not in the presence of the accused, and is not tested by cross-examination.

Normally, when the High Court believes the evidence given by the eye witnesses, the Supreme Court accepts the appraisal of the evidence by that court and does not examine the evidence afresh for itself.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the evidentiary value of a dying declaration is not destroyed simply because the original document was stolen from the court file. The contents of the declaration can be sufficiently proven by the testimony of the Judicial Magistrate who recorded it. Similarly, the value of the declaration is not diminished by the fact that an investigating officer was allowed to make a copy of it.
legal_tests_applied: A dying declaration stands on the same footing as another piece of evidence and has to be judged in the light of surrounding circumstances and with reference to the principles governing the weighing of evidence.

The weak points of a dying declaration, such as not being made under oath or subject to cross-examination, serve to put the court on its guard, imposing an obligation to closely scrutinise all attendant circumstances to test its reliability.
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that the stolen original destroyed the dying declaration's value because the Judicial Magistrate who recorded it provided evidence as to its contents.
The court held that the fact that the investigating officer was allowed to make a copy of the dying declaration did not diminish its evidentiary value.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's position was upheld because the court accepted the testimony of the Judicial Magistrate as sufficient proof of the contents of the missing dying declaration.
The court found no legal fault in the investigating officer having made a copy of the declaration that would justify reducing its evidentiary weight.
policy_considerations: The reasoning implies a policy that the course of justice should not be frustrated by the theft or loss of a court document when its contents can be reliably established through other credible evidence, such as the testimony of the judicial officer who created it.
